newsitem.title: USA: EchoStar, News Corp. venture dealt a blow.
newsitem.headline: EchoStar, News Corp. venture dealt a blow.

text.p: Yet another blow was dealt Friday to the pending billion-dollar direct-TV satellite deal between EchoStar Communications Corp. and News Corp Ltd. with the resignation of one of the venture's top executives.

Preston Padden, the head of News Corp.'s ASkyB satellite TV service who was involved in negotiations with EchoStar, submitted his resignation, News Corp. said, casting further doubt on plans to launch the venture.
"With Padden resigning, it just doesn't seem like the soldiers are in place to get this thing back on track," said Ted Henderson, managing director of research at Janco Partners.
News Corp. spokesman Jim Platt maintained Padden's resignation would have no effect on the venture.

"It doesn't mean anything," Platt said in an interview. "It has no effect on that." News Corp. Chairman Rupert Murdoch was quoted by The Wall Street Journal as saying he was pushing ahead with plans to launch a satellite-television service -- with or without EchoStar.
"We're going ahead, either on our own or with (EchoStar Chairman Charles Ergen) if he meets the terms of the contract," Murdoch was quoted as saying.

The deal, which was announced in February, began to unravel earlier this week when EchoStar announced it would be delaying regulatory filings related to the deal because of a dispute over the conditional-access system that would be used.
EchoStar said News Corp. was pushing for it to abandon the current system it uses in favour of one owned by News Corp.
A critical component of the direct-broadcast satellite industry is the conditional-access system, an encryption service that allows subscribers to view only those channels for which they have paid.

Under the alliance, News Corp. was to invest $1 billion in a jointly run system offering as many as 500 channels of digital TV, Internet services and local broadcast TV signals to markets across the United States.

Aside from apparent difficulties between the two companies, the venture has run into other stumbling blocks. In particular, it must pass antitrust muster, foreign ownership questions and U.S. copyright laws.
There also have been reports that Murdoch had approached Tele-Communications Inc. Chairman John Malone about a possible alliance with Primestar, a satellite partnership made up of six companies.
As a result, Padden's departure was viewed by some analysts as yet another sign the alliance could dissolve -- and further encourage Murdoch to try to cut a deal with another partner.
"It doesn't sound like a great start for a marriage," NatWest Securities analyst Gary Farber said.
Aside from the February announcement of the deal, "there doesn't appear to be any positive news flow on this venture," Farber said. "It's in flux."
